blocks.text: Reuse behavior by holding collaborators and delegating to them, rather than extending a class and inheriting its internals.

Inheritance couples a subclass to the parent's **implementation**, including the calls the parent makes to its own overridable methods. **Composition** couples you only to a public contract, can change at runtime and lets one object use several behaviors. Inherit only for a true is-a that the parent was designed to support.

items: **Fragile base class:** a parent change breaks children.
**Forwarding:** the wrapper uses only the declared contract.
**One parent only:** a class extends once but can hold many collaborators.

blocks.text: Effective Java's advice: design and document for inheritance, or prohibit it. Most classes should be `final` or sealed.

walkthrough.note: `CountingSetBefore` extends `HashSet` and counts in `add` and `addAll`. But `HashSet.addAll` already calls `add`, so each element is counted twice.
The wrapper holds the set instead of extending it. `addAll` loops over its own `add`, so counting depends only on code we control.
Everything else forwards to `inner`. The class promises the `Set` contract and nothing about how `HashSet` is implemented.
Same calls, different answers: inheritance reports 6 for three elements, composition 3. The wrapper also accepts any `Set`, such as a `TreeSet`.

blocks.text: An `Enemy` hierarchy grew `FlyingEnemy`, `FireEnemy` and `FlyingFireEnemy`, and designers then asked for ice-breathing flyers that can be frozen. Behaviors were extracted into `Movement` and `Attack` components held by a single `Enemy`. A new enemy is configuration, not a class, and a frozen enemy swaps its movement at runtime.

lines: record Enemy(String name, Movement move, Attack attack) {}
var dragon = new Enemy("dragon", new Fly(8), new Breath(FIRE));
var frozen = new Enemy(dragon.name(), new Stuck(), dragon.attack());

blocks.text: Payoff: N movements and M attacks cost N + M classes, not N times M.

lists.title: Use when
items: Behavior varies along several independent axes.
The parent is not designed for extension or lives in another library.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: There is a genuine, documented is-a in a hierarchy you own, such as an abstract skeleton.
The interface is wide and hand-written forwarding adds little.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: The self-use problem: a wrapped object that passes `this` bypasses the wrapper.
New `default` methods are inherited, not forwarded, so the inner object's overrides are bypassed.
Sharing a mutable collaborator between several wrappers.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A wrapper that forwards everything and adds nothing.
Long delegate chains that hide who does the work.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Records, sealed interfaces and lambdas make small collaborators cheap.
Java has no built-in delegation; IDEs generate the forwarding methods.

rows.difference: Decorator is composition with the same interface: it wraps an object to add behavior while remaining substitutable.
A strategy is a swappable collaborator held by composition, the standard replacement for subclass-per-variant.
Template Method reuses an algorithm skeleton through inheritance, fixed at compile time; composition varies it at runtime.
Bridge uses composition to split abstraction from implementation so both hierarchies vary independently.
Avoiding implementation inheritance avoids most substitutability traps that LSP describes.

entries.name: Thread with Runnable
entries.detail: Pass a `Runnable` to `Thread` instead of subclassing it; the task is composed in.

entries.name: java.io BufferedInputStream
entries.detail: Wraps any `InputStream` and adds buffering; it holds the stream rather than extending a specific one.

entries.name: Collections.synchronizedList
entries.detail: Returns a wrapper that forwards to the given list under a lock, adding behavior by composition.

entries.name: java.util.Stack
entries.detail: Extends `Vector`, exposing indexed access that breaks stack discipline: a widely cited inheritance mistake.

exercises.prompt: Which guideline does this class most clearly ignore?
lines: // addAll, set, addFirst... all remain unaudited

options.why: It extends a concrete collection to bolt on behavior, inheriting a large surface it cannot fully control.
`AuditedList` still behaves as a list; the issue is brittle reuse, not substitutability.
`ArrayList` is not a fat interface that this class is forced to implement.
The class has one purpose; its flaw is how it reuses `ArrayList`.

exercises.scenario: You need an HTTP client with retries and metrics today, and caching and tracing next quarter, in varying combinations per service. A colleague proposes `RetryingMetricsHttpClient extends BaseHttpClient`.

options.why: Wrap one `HttpClient` in small decorators (retry, metrics, cache) and combine them per service; no combinatorial subclasses.
Subclasses can stay substitutable, but the number of combinations still explodes.
Separating concerns helps, but SRP alone does not say how to combine them.
Depending on an interface is good, but it does not solve the combination problem.

exercises.prompt: Tap the line that couples the class to an implementation.
lines: final class UserCache extends HashMap<String, User> {
exercises.explanation: A cache has a map; it is not one. Extending exposes `put`, `putAll` and `clear`, so callers bypass the capacity rule. Hold a `Map` in a private field and expose only `find`, `remember` and `evictInactive`.

exercises.explanation: Build the delegate, wrap it, perform the operation, then read the counter the wrapper maintained.

template: class CountingSet<E> { CountingSet(Set<E> s) {} void addAll(Collection<E> c) {} int added() { return 0; } }

exercises.prompt: Explain 'composition over inheritance' in your own words. Why did the `HashSet.addAll` double count happen?

modelAnswer.text: Inheritance ties a subclass to the parent's implementation, including self-calls between its methods. HashSet.addAll calls add, so a subclass counting in both counts each element twice. Holding a Set and forwarding depends only on its contract, avoids that coupling, and lets behavior be combined or swapped at runtime.

keyPoints: Inheritance couples to implementation, composition to contract
Self-use of overridable methods causes double counting
Wrapper forwards and controls its own paths
Composition allows runtime swapping and multiple behaviors
